title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, which is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.
shortTitle: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree — recursive DFS

s1_definition.profdef: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree is computed with a recursive depth-first traversal where each node's depth is one plus the greater of its left and right subtree depths. The recursion bottoms out at null children, which contribute a depth of zero, and the value returned at the root is the longest root-to-leaf path length counted in nodes.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the bank's organizational hierarchy as a tree, with the branch manager at the top and reporting chains going down. The maximum depth is the longest chain of command from the manager down to the most junior employee. To measure it, each manager asks their two deputies how deep their own sub-teams go, takes the deeper of the two, and adds one for themselves. The number that bubbles up to the top is the longest chain in the whole branch.
s1_definition.oneliner: The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its two children, and an empty child contributes zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree is computed with a recursive depth-first traversal where each node's depth is one plus the greater of its left and right subtree depths. The recursion bottoms out at null children, which contribute a depth of zero, and the value returned at the root is the longest root-to-leaf path length counted in nodes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the bank's organizational hierarchy as a tree, with the branch manager at the top and reporting chains going down. The maximum depth is the longest chain of command from the manager down to the most junior employee. To measure it, each manager asks their two deputies how deep their own sub-teams go, takes the deeper of the two, and adds one for themselves. The number that bubbles up to the top is the longest chain in the whole branch.

**One line to remember:** The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its two children, and an empty child contributes zero.

sections.s2_technical:
A binary tree node has a value and up to two children, left and right. Depth is naturally recursive because the depth of a tree is defined in terms of the depth of its subtrees. This is a classic post-order style computation: you need the children's answers before you can compute the parent's.

The base case is a null node, which has depth zero. For example: `if (node == null) return 0;`. This single line handles empty trees and the bottoms of every branch.

The recursive case asks each child for its depth and combines them. For example: `int left = maxDepth(node.left); int right = maxDepth(node.right); return 1 + Math.max(left, right);`. The plus one counts the current node itself, and taking the maximum ensures you follow the longer of the two branches.

The time complexity is linear in the number of nodes because every node is visited exactly once. The space complexity is proportional to the height of the tree because of the recursion call stack; in the worst case of a completely skewed tree this is linear, and in a balanced tree it is logarithmic.

A senior nuance is the alternative iterative approach using breadth-first search with a queue, counting the number of levels. This avoids deep recursion and the risk of a stack overflow on a pathologically skewed tree with millions of nodes. For example, you process the tree level by level and increment a depth counter once per level. Knowing both the elegant recursive form and the stack-safe iterative form, and when each is appropriate, is the senior-level answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy for large loans is modeled as a binary tree of approvers, where each approver may escalate to up to two higher authorities. The compliance team needs the longest escalation chain, because a very deep chain means a loan could take too many approval hops and breach the service-level agreement. This is exactly how Maximum Depth works — it measures the longest root-to-leaf path.

Problem 2 — The hierarchy is built dynamically and can be unbalanced, so the measurement must handle both shallow and very deep chains correctly, including empty branches. This is exactly why the recursion treats a null child as depth zero and takes the maximum of the two sides.

The mini-project builds an `ApproverNode` class representing a node in the approval tree, a `HierarchyDepthService` with a recursive `maxDepth` method and logging, and a runnable demo that builds a small approval hierarchy and measures its longest chain.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the approval tree rooted at BranchManager.

Step 1: The service calls maxDepth on BranchManager. To answer, it must first find the depth of its left child CreditOfficer and its right child RiskHead.

Step 2: It recurses into CreditOfficer, which has a left child JuniorAnalyst and no right child. JuniorAnalyst has no children, so both its recursive calls hit null and return zero, making JuniorAnalyst's depth one plus zero equals one. CreditOfficer's left is one and its right is zero, so CreditOfficer's depth is one plus one equals two.

Step 3: It recurses into RiskHead, which has no left child and a right child RegionalVP. RegionalVP has no left child and a right child NationalHead. NationalHead has no children, so its depth is one. RegionalVP's depth is one plus max of zero and one equals two. RiskHead's depth is one plus max of zero and two equals three.

Step 4: Back at BranchManager, the left depth is two and the right depth is three. BranchManager's depth is one plus max of two and three equals four.

Step 5: The service logs that the longest escalation chain depth is four. Since four is not greater than four, the SLA warning does not fire.

```text
2026-10-26T17:30:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Loan Approval Chain Depth
2026-10-26T17:30:00Z [INFO] Longest approval escalation chain depth = 4
```

```text
              BranchManager  depth = 1 + max(2,3) = 4
             /              \
   CreditOfficer(2)       RiskHead(3)
        │                      \
  JuniorAnalyst(1)          RegionalVP(2)
     (leaf)                      \
                              NationalHead(1)
                                 (leaf)

  Recursion returns bubble UP:
    NationalHead → 1
    RegionalVP   → 1+max(0,1)=2
    RiskHead     → 1+max(0,2)=3
    JuniorAnalyst→ 1
    CreditOfficer→ 1+max(1,0)=2
    BranchManager→ 1+max(2,3)=4  ← answer
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree is the cleanest example of a recursive definition that translates directly into code, because the depth of a tree is naturally one plus the greater of its two subtree depths. My solution is a depth-first recursion with a single base case: a null node has depth zero. For any real node I ask both children for their depths, take the larger of the two to follow the longer branch, and add one to count the current node.

This is a post-order computation in spirit, because a parent cannot know its depth until both children have reported theirs. Taking the maximum of the two sides is what guarantees I measure the longest root-to-leaf path rather than some arbitrary branch, and treating a missing child as zero is what makes unbalanced and empty trees fall out correctly without special cases.

The time complexity is linear because every node is visited once, and the space complexity is proportional to the height of the tree because of the recursion stack, which is logarithmic for a balanced tree but linear for a completely skewed one. For very deep trees I would switch to an iterative breadth-first approach that counts levels, which avoids any risk of a stack overflow, and knowing when to prefer that stack-safe form is the senior-level point.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this to measure the longest escalation chain in a loan approval hierarchy modeled as a binary tree of approvers. A chain that is too deep means a loan could take too many approval hops and breach the service-level agreement, so the recursion returns the longest chain length and the service raises a warning when it exceeds the allowed threshold.
